## Scope

`curelearning` is designed for right-censored studies in which the scientific
target is long-term event-free survival. For a fixed window, the directly
identified target is an average of the population survival tail. It equals a
cure fraction only when residual susceptible survival over that window is
negligible. It is not an observed subject-level cure label, and it requires
adequate follow-up.

The package supplies:

1. `survcure()`, an honest cure-fraction survival tree;
2. `randomforestcure()`, a randomized ensemble of honest trees;
3. matched log-rank splitting through `splitrule = "logrank"`;
4. population, susceptible, and dynamic-cure predictions from trees and forests;
5. neighbor-based late survival prediction (`cureknn()`) and boosting models.

## Simulated long-term survival data

The following small example has one variable that changes the cure fraction
and one variable that changes event timing among susceptible subjects.

```{r data}
library(survival)
library(curelearning)

set.seed(2401)
n <- 600
x_cure <- runif(n)
x_latency <- factor(rbinom(n, 1, 0.5), labels = c("slow", "fast"))
noise <- rnorm(n)

pi0 <- plogis(-0.8 + 3.0 * (x_cure - 0.5))
long_term <- rbinom(n, 1, pi0)
rate <- ifelse(x_latency == "fast", 0.35, 0.14)
susceptible_time <- pmin(rexp(n, rate), 9)
event_time <- ifelse(long_term == 1, Inf, susceptible_time)
censor_time <- runif(n, 0, 12)

dat <- data.frame(
  time = pmin(event_time, censor_time),
  status = as.integer(event_time <= censor_time),
  x_cure = x_cure,
  x_latency = x_latency,
  noise = noise
)
```

## Predict survival from comparable patients

The fitted horizons are in the same units as `time`. The two new patients provide baseline predictors only. When the neighbors do not have enough follow-up, `predict()` gives a reason instead of a numerical survival estimate.

```{r knn}
knn <- cureknn(Surv(time, status) ~ x_cure + x_latency + noise, dat,
               times = c(7, 8, 9), k = c(50, 100), seed = 11)
patients <- data.frame(x_cure = c(0.25, 0.75), x_latency = c("slow", "fast"), noise = 0)
predict(knn, patients)
head(predict(knn, patients, type = "neighbors"))
```

## Fit an honest tree

The 7--9 year window is specified before fitting. Both daughter nodes must
retain adequate risk-set support in this interval.

```{r tree}
tree <- curetree(
  Surv(time, status) ~ x_cure + x_latency + noise,
  data = dat,
  tail.start = 7,
  tail.end = 9,
  nodesize = 30,
  min.tail.at.risk = 8,
  min.tail.end.at.risk = 3,
  maxdepth = 2,
  nsplit = 8,
  seed = 11
)
tree
summary(tree)
```

The estimated cure probability and population survival are available through
the standard `predict()` generic.

```{r tree-predict}
predict(tree, dat[1:6, ], type = "cure")
predict(tree, dat[1:3, ], type = "survival", times = c(3, 6, 9))
```

## Fit a cure-fraction forest

This vignette uses 20 trees for speed. Analyses ordinarily use a larger
ensemble and should examine stability across random seeds.

```{r forest}
forest <- cureforest(
  Surv(time, status) ~ x_cure + x_latency + noise,
  data = dat,
  ntree = 20,
  mtry = 2,
  nodesize = 25,
  maxdepth = 2,
  nsplit = 8,
  tail.start = 7,
  tail.end = 9,
  min.tail.at.risk = 7,
  min.tail.end.at.risk = 3,
  n.cores = 1,
  seed = 22
)
forest
cure_importance(forest)
```

```{r forest-predict}
pred <- predict(forest, dat[1:4, ], type = "all", times = c(3, 6, 9))
pred$cure
pred$survival
pred$susceptible
pred$dynamic
```

## Matched log-rank comparison

Use the same tree controls with `splitrule = "logrank"` to isolate the effect
of the splitting target. A generic predictive advantage should not be assumed:
the comparison asks whether cure-oriented splitting creates different,
tail-supported strata.

```{r matched-comparison}
logrank_tree <- curetree(
  Surv(time, status) ~ x_cure + x_latency + noise,
  data = dat,
  splitrule = "logrank",
  tail.start = 7,
  tail.end = 9,
  nodesize = 30,
  min.tail.at.risk = 8,
  min.tail.end.at.risk = 3,
  maxdepth = 2,
  nsplit = 8,
  seed = 11
)

summary(tree)$splits
summary(logrank_tree)$splits
```

## Held-out comparison with a standard random survival forest

`cure_latency_demo` is included with the package, so the complete comparison
requires no external files or preprocessing. Here the proposed model and the
ordinary log-rank random survival forest are fitted explicitly before both
objects are evaluated on the prespecified test cohort.

```{r rsf-comparison, eval=FALSE}
data(cure_latency_demo)
train <- subset(cure_latency_demo, cohort == "train")
test <- subset(cure_latency_demo, cohort == "test")
form <- Surv(time, event) ~
  cure_marker + latency_marker + age + stage + biomarker + noise

fit.cure <- cureforest(
  form, train, ntree = 200, mtry = 6, nodesize = 80, maxdepth = 1,
  tail.start = 7, tail.end = 9.5, n.cores = 6, seed = 20260725
)
fit.rsf <- randomForestSRC::rfsrc(
  form, train, ntree = 200, mtry = 6, nodesize = 80, nodedepth = 1,
  splitrule = "logrank", nthread = 6, seed = 20260725
)

predict(fit.cure, test, type = "cure")
benchmark <- compare_forest_fits(fit.cure, fit.rsf, test, n.cores = 6)
benchmark$performance
```

The benchmark is deliberately shallow: it isolates the effect of asking each
split to target cure or event-time separation. It is an explanatory example,
not an empirical claim that one forest must dominate the other in every data
set. The reported table contains the held-out C-index for both methods,
together with Brier scores and IBS.

## Optional finite-horizon curve refinement

`curecurveboost()` first fits a CureForest anchor, then refines its implied
susceptible curve using time-dependent log-hazard trees. Anchor fitting,
correction fitting, early stopping, and final acceptance use disjoint samples.
By default, half the validation pool selects one candidate and the other half
accepts it only if a one-sided paired lower bound for Brier improvement is
positive. Otherwise the round-zero curve is retained. The correction
does not impose proportional hazards and does not change the tail estimate.

```{r flexible-refinement, eval=FALSE}
refined <- curecurveboost(
  Surv(time, status) ~ x_cure + x_latency + noise, dat,
  breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9),
  forest.control = list(tail.start = 7, tail.end = 9), seed = 11
)
predict(refined, dat[1:5, ], times = c(3, 5, 8))
predict(refined, dat[1:5, ], type = "cure")  # unchanged anchor
refined$gate                              # why correction was accepted/rejected
```

Use `selection = "minimum"` to reproduce the previous selection rule. The
independent acceptance sample must not be reused to search among additional
models. Its t-based bound is approximate and is not a finite-sample guarantee
that harmful changes never occur.

This is a development-stage predictive refinement, not an inferential
extension of the forest theorems. No extrapolation beyond the last boundary
is provided. Its benefit must be checked on a separate test sample against
both the uncorrected forest and an appropriately tuned, unrestricted RSF.
Use `outcome = "train"` for RSF prediction, preferably supplying predictors
only: `outcome = "test"` recomputes leaf estimates from test outcomes and is
not a locked-model out-of-sample comparison.

## Reporting recommendations

Report the prespecified tail window, numbers at risk at its beginning and end,
terminal fallback frequency, and sensitivity to alternative scientifically
reasonable windows. Prediction metrics complement these diagnostics but do not
replace them.
